text: Sex identification and efficient microsatellite genotyping using fecal DNA in proboscis monkeys (Nasalis larvatus)

Genetic sex identification and efficient microsatellite genotyping using non-invasive samples are important for assessing genetic diversity and structure of wild mammals. We extracted DNA from fecal samples of endangered proboscis monkeys (Nasalis larvatus) at the Yokohama Zoological Gardens, and successfully identified their sex using a DEAD-box gene marker. Using the information of 31 published microsatellite loci developed for proboscis monkeys, we redesigned the primers for 18 loci and selected microsatellite loci with high heterozygosities and then developed a multiplex PCR system, in which 19 polymorphic microsatellite loci and a sex identification marker were amplified in three multiplex sets. In our developed method, genotyping errors rarely happened using DNA extracted from feces, and we could identify individuals and estimate parent-offspring relationship with high confidence. Our developed method is applicable for genetic analysis of wild proboscis monkeys and will provide us the information of not only their ecological and social features but also conservation management.

In endangered wild mammals, genetic sex identification and efficient microsatellite genotyping using noninvasive samples, such as feces, are essential for assessment of genetic diversity and structure as well as effective management (Lampa et al. 2013). In addition, genetic sex/ individual identification of fecal samples is important to support further understanding of their ecological traits; as feces can provide ecologically important information, e.g., diet or gut microbes (Tutin and Fernandez 1985;Ley et al. 2008), we can analyze sex/individual difference in such information in combination with genetic sex/individual identification. The endangered proboscis monkey (Nasalis larvatus), a member of the Old World monkey subfamily Colobinae, is found only on the island of Borneo. They are the largest foregut-fermenting Asian colobine and ingest a diet consisting of various leaves and fruits (Matsuda et al. 2009;Matsuda et al. 2015). Because their preferred habitats, i.e., peat swamp and mangrove forests, are constantly or periodically inundated (Salter et al. 1985; Bennett and Sebastian 1988;Yeager 1989; but see Boonratana 2000 andMatsuda et al. 2009 for riverine forests), knowledge of their ecology based on direct observation is still limited. In addition, proboscis monkeys might create a special social system so-called 'multilevel society', in which smaller levels of social organization, i.e., one-male-multifemale units, aggregate into larger units at their sleeping sites (Yeager 1991: Grueter et al. 2012; but see Matsuda et al. 2012). However, genetic relationships of individuals within and among units of these species are largely unknown. Thus, genetic analyses using noninvasive fecal samples are important for not only the knowledge of their ecological and social features but also conservation strategies.
When genetic sex identification was conducted using noninvasive samples, co-amplification of homologous X-Y regions was thought to be better than Y specific markers, such as SRY, because of a low polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification rate (Yamauchi et al. 2000;Fernando and Melnick 2001). Villesen and Fredsted (2006) reported that a part of the DEAD-box gene located in the sex chromosome could identify the sex in many primate species, including the red-shanked douc (Pygathrix nemaeus), which is phylogenetically close to proboscis monkeys (Liedigk et al. 2012). This marker might be useful for the genetic sex identification of proboscis monkeys. Salgado-Lynn et al. (2010) reported microsatellite primers for proboscis monkeys, some of which produced clear amplification using fecal samples. Co-amplification of multiple markers in the same tube, called multiplex PCR, can greatly reduce the costs and amount of template DNA required. To conduct an effective genotyping using fecal samples, it is essential to develop a multiplex PCR system in which a sufficient number of microsatellite loci can be amplified for kinship analysis with a low number of multiplex sets. Moreover, pilot studies are recommended for obtaining reliable genotypes from fecal samples (Lampa et al. 2013). This is because DNA extracted from fecal samples can lead to PCR failure or genotyping errors, such as allelic dropout and false alleles (Pompanon et al. 2005). Therefore, it is important to calculate genotyping error rates before analysis of wild samples.
First, we performed sex identification using the fecal samples of proboscis monkeys at the Yokohama Zoological Gardens. Second, we selected microsatellite markers which produced clear results using fecal samples and were highly polymorphic from the published markers (Salgado-Lynn et al. 2010), and then developed a multiplex PCR system including a sex identification marker. Third, we calculated PCR error rates by also using DNA extracted from blood samples. In addition, we tested whether the selected markers had enough diversity for kinship analysis. Finally, using our developed method, we re-assessed the genetic diversity of captive proboscis monkeys as described in Ogata and Seino (2015).

In July and August 2014, we collected fecal samples from five proboscis monkeys (No. 1, 2, 3, 5, and 6) at the Yokohama Zoological Gardens. No. 1 and 2 were adult females, No. 3 was a young adult male, No. 5 was an adult male, and No. 6 was an offspring of No. 1 and 5. Pedigree data of the five founder individuals (No. 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5) were not available (Ogata and Seino 2015). We scrubbed the surface of feces with cotton swabs and stored them in 2 ml tubes with 1 ml lysis buffer consisting of 0.5% SDS, 100 mM EDTA, 100 mM Tris-HCl, and 10 mM NaCl (Longmire et al. 1997) at room temperature for ca. 110 days after collection until DNA extraction. DNA was extracted using QIAamp DNA Stool Mini Kit ( Qiagen). We also used DNA extracted from blood samples of five proboscis monkeys (No. 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5) for positive controls (Ogata and Seino 2015). Although fecal samples of No. 4, which was a young adult male, were not available because of the absence of the individual at the sampling time, we analyzed the genotype of this individual for kinship analysis.

We amplified a part of the DEAD-box gene using a primer pair (NED labeled F-Deadbox1 and R-Deadbox1) as described in Villesen and Fredsted (2006). The expected fragment sizes of X and Y are 180 bp and 209 bp, respectively (Villesen and Fredsted 2006).

First, we tested 20 microsatellite markers (NID10, NID5, NIE10, NIF1, NIP1A6, NIP1C3, NIP1C5, NIP1F5, NIP2B9, NIP2C12, NIP2D6, NIP2F3, NIP3B2, NIP3E7, NIP3G2, NIP4B1, NIP4B2, NIP4C6, NIP4C11, and NIP4E6) that were reported to be successfully amplified using fecal DNA with fluorescently labeled (FAM, HEX, NED) primers (Salgado-Lynn et al. 2010). If PCR amplifications produced ambiguous results or included many non-specific bands, new primers were designed based on registered sequences using Primer 3 (Koressaar and Remm 2007;Untergrasser et al. 2012). We redesigned primer sets to increase variety of expected allele lengths of microsatellite loci, which improved the development of the multiplex system.
We also tested 16 loci (NIG8, NIP1C8, NIP1E9, NIP1F2, NIP1G7, NIP2B8, NIP2C5, NIP2F7, NIP3A12, NIP3B4, NIP3B6, NIP3C11, NIP3E1, NIP3E8, NIP3H5, and NIP4E10), which were reported to result in poor amplification using fecal DNA (Salgado-Lynn et al. 2010), to increase the number of loci with high variation. We designed new primer sets for nine of the 16 loci to increase the variety in expected allele lengths. Newly designed primer sequences are summarized in Table 1. When we conducted the initial screening of these markers, an economic method which added an M13 (-21) sequence tail at the 5' end of forward primers was used for the fluorescent labeling of the PCR fragments (Schuelke 2000).

All the PCR amplification including sex identification was carried out in 5 µl reactions containing 0.2 mM of each primer, 2.5 ml of QIAGEN Multiplex PCR Master Mix (Qiagen), and 2 ml of fecal DNA or 1 ml of bloodderived DNA. In multiplex PCR, we modified concentra-  tion of several primers (Table 2). After an initial incubation at 95°C for 15 min, PCR amplification was performed for 45 cycles consisting of denaturation at 94°C for 30 sec, annealing at 57°C for 30 sec, extension at 72°C for 30 sec, and a final extension at 60°C for 30 min. The amplification products were separated with capillary electrophoresis using an ABI 3130xl Genetic Analyzer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Alleles were sized using Peak Scanner Software v1.0 (Thermo Fisher Scientific).
The primer combination in a multiplex PCR system was assessed with Multiplex Manager v1.2 (Holleley and Geerts 2009). To calculate the PCR failure rate, multiplex PCR amplification was conducted twice per sample using five fecal samples.

We calculated the observed and expected heterozygosity using GenAlEx 6.3 (Peakall and Smouse 2006). We also calculated PIsibs, which indicates the probability that sibling pairs will have the same genotype opportu nistically, using GenAlEx 6.3. This parameter is a good indicator of the accuracy of individual identifi- Parentage analysis was conducted using CERVUS 3.0 (Kalinowski et al. 2007). Relatedness was estimated with the Trio-ML estimator using COANCESTRY 1.0 (Wang 2011). The ML-Relate software (Kalinowski et al. 2006) was used for estimating four pedigree relationships: unrelated, half-siblings, full-siblings, and parent-offspring. We used the allele frequency without No. 6 for all kinship analyses because relatives could strongly affect the allele frequency in a small sample size.
Allelic dropout rate in each locus was calculated as the number of observed dropouts divided by the total number of amplifications of individuals determined as heterozygous genotypes.

We successfully identified the sex using a DEAD-box gene marker in proboscis monkeys. Two female and three male DNA samples extracted from fecal samples produced 180/180 and 180/210 genotypes, respectively.

Among the 20 microsatellite loci reported to be successfully amplified using fecal DNA, PCR amplification in 11 loci produced clear results without non-specific alleles. We designed new primer sets for the other nine loci (Table 1), and the new primers produced clear results. Even among the 16 loci reported to have poor amplification using fecal DNA, PCR amplification with 11 loci produced clear results. The characteristics of the 31 loci that produced clear results using five fecal samples are shown in Table 2. From them, we removed six monomorphic loci and five loci in which either the observed or expected heterozygosity was low (< 0.2).
For 20 polymorphic markers combined with a NED labeled DEAD-box primer pair, we tested multiplex PCR with three PCR sets (Table 2). Although the NIP3A12 locus was not efficiently amplified, the other 19 microsatellite loci and a sex identification marker produced the same genotypes as those obtained by singleplex PCRs, except for two allelic dropout cases (NIP2C12 and NIP4E6). The allelic dropout rate was 0.013 (2/150) in total (Table 2). Other genotyping errors, such as no amplification or false genotypes, were not observed. The accumulated PIsibs value of 19 microsatellite loci in three sets and seven loci in only set 1 was 1.9 × 10 -6 and 4.6 × 10 -3 , respectively.
We also conducted multiplex PCR with five DNA samples extracted from blood samples. The genotypes obtained from four overlapping individuals were the same as those obtained from fecal samples.

We used the genotypes of six individuals in 19 microsatellite loci of three multiplex sets for kinship analysis. Individual No. 6 shared one allele with the mother (No. 1) and another allele with the father (No. 5) at all loci. Parent pair analysis (sexes known) using CERVUS 3.0 showed that the mother and the father of No. 6 were estimated to be No. 1 and 5, respectively, with high confidence (99%).
Relatedness estimates by TrioML in No. 1-No. 6 and No. 5-No. 6 pairs were 0.5 and 0.41, respectively (Table 3). Both pairs were estimated to be parent-offspring by ML-Relate analysis (Table 3).

This is the first study to successfully apply genetic sex identification in proboscis monkeys. A DEAD-box gene marker has been successfully applied to closely-related species of proboscis monkey, including red-shanked douc (Villesen and Fredsted 2006) and Sichuan snub-nosed monkeys (Chang et al. 2012). Therefore, this marker may be useful for the genetic sex identification of species of the subfamily Colobinae, even using noninvasive samples.

section: informative multiplex pcr system of microsatellite loci
text:
In our developed methods, 19 microsatellite loci and a sex identification marker produced clear results in only three multiplex sets, although consistent amplification of fecal samples from proboscis monkeys was not possible using the multiplex approach described by Salgado-Lynn et al. (2010). One of the reasons for the difference in the success rate might be different sampling methods of the fecal samples between two studies. Specifically, Salgado-Lynn et al. ( 2010) sampled whole feces stored in 70% ethanol, whereas our study sampled only the fecal surface stored in lysis buffer. Sampling only the fecal surface has been reported to be a good method for the noninvasive genetic studies of mammals (Wehausen et al. 2004;Stenglein et al. 2010;Inoue 2015). Further, the low rate of genotyping errors in our study also suggests that the surface collection method is efficient for mammalian genotyping.
In this study, we demonstrated that redesigning primer sets was useful for noninvasive genotyping. PCR amplification with fecal samples occasionally failed even on using primer pairs that produced clear results with invasive samples, such as tissues (Salgado-Lynn et al. 2010), probably because primer matching might be more important using noninvasive samples. In addition, redesigning primers could be important for developing multiplex systems. Allele length variation in microsatellite loci could decrease the number of multiplex sets. Thus, we recommend the redesigning of primers prior to optimizing a multiplex system if PCR amplifications in some loci do not produce clear results using noninvasive samples or the allele lengths of markers overlap.
The genetic diversity of 19 microsatellite loci in three multiplex sets was high enough to identify the parentage of zoo proboscis monkeys. The genetic diversity of eight microsatellite loci was reported using the feces of 29 wild proboscis monkeys (Table 2, Salgado-Lynn et al. 2010). Although only five individuals were used in our study, expected heterozygosities in the study conducted by Salgado-Lynn et al. (2010) were almost the same as those in our data, except for two loci (ExNID10 and NIP2F3) that have low diversity in our study. This finding suggests that the genetic diversity information obtained in our study is similar to, or at least not higher, compared to the wild population. The low accumulated PIsibs values of seven loci in multiplex set 1 (4.6 × 10 -3 ) suggest that we can identify individuals only using this set. Population size estimation based on noninvasive genetic markrecapture has been widely applied in mammals (Lampa et al. 2013). Therefore, effective genetic individual identification in this study may help us to assess the population size of proboscis monkeys.
The PCR failure rate is important to be assessed for noninvasive genetics (Pompanon et al. 2005). In our study, we observed a low rate of allelic dropout, and other PCR failures were not observed. When we used a 1.3% allelic dropout rate to calculate the number of repetitions necessary to correctly determine homozygous genotypes with 99% certainty, two replicates (0.013) 2 were found to be sufficient. This information will be valuable for analyzing samples of wild proboscis monkeys in the future. As similar to the condition in this study, fresh fecal samples (< 2 h after defecation) are possibly collected in the early morning when proboscis monkeys leave their sleeping trees (Matsuda et al. 2014), and thus genotyping errors may not much differ between wild and captive populations.

CERVUS and ML-Relate showed that our developed multiplex sets enabled us to estimate parent-offspring relationship with high confidence as suggested in Inoue et al. (2013), which showed that kinship analyses accurately assigned related dyads to the appropriate relatedness category, r = 0.5, using 16 microsatellite markers in wild gorillas. Thus, our results suggest that genotypes from our method are sufficient to conduct parentage analysis with high accuracy, even using a wild population.

section: genetic information of proboscis monkeys at the zoo
text: The genetic information of endangered species kept at the zoo is important for their management. A previous study assessed the genetic diversity and kinship using mitochondria and four microsatellite loci of five proboscis monkeys at the Yokohama Zoological Gardens (Ogata and Seino 2015). Using our multiplex methods including 19 microsatellite loci, we showed a relatively high genetic diversity of proboscis monkeys kept at the zoo, similar to that observed in a previous report (Ogata and Seino 2015). The ML-Relate estimated that the relationship between No. 2 and 5, which was suggested to be genetically related by Ogata and Seino (2015), was full-siblings (Table 3). The Trio-ML relatedness estimate in that pair was also high (0.29, Table 3). Moreover, these two individuals were reported to share a haplotype of the mitochondrial control region (Ogata and Seino 2015), and the age difference between these individuals was only one year. Although dyadic kinship assignments based on analyses involving fewer than 30 microsatellite loci are reported to be unreliable (Blouin 2003), our results indicate that the No. 2-No. 5 pair might be a maternal half-sibling or fullsibling pair.
